rule: good. context only and never parsed; text 2 is the clean carrier of this rule, while texts 1, 3 and 4 need the edits below.
texts: mixed: nothing is lost and the rule fires, but the derived attracting is keyed to the lantern and its mist-light rather than to the occasion, so two separate showings by the same lantern collapse into one single attracting event. Use the instruction set's own per-occasion wording so each showing gets its own attracting: 'Every time a lantern shows mist-light at night, the mist-light attracts nightmoths.'
good. the showing, the at-night condition and the attracting all parse, with the response tied to each individual showing.

mixed: the denial itself is right and reaches any nightmoth and any ordinary firelight, but the parse never records that a nightmoth is a moth or that firelight is a light, so both coinages sit in the knowledge base unconnected to their genus — and your other nightmoth sentences do record that link, so the two disagree. Hyphenating the two solid-spelled coinages makes the modifier-plus-head structure explicit, which is what that genus link keys on: 'Night-moths do not see ordinary fire-light.'

bad: 'a night is cold' states a condition but describes no happening, so the rule has no occasion to hang the flying on; the derived flying comes out unrestricted, claiming nightmoths rarely fly at all rather than rarely on cold nights. Fold the condition into the clause it restricts so it stays attached to the flying: 'Nightmoths rarely fly on a cold night.'
